docs.title: Flow Unofficial Documentation
docs.text:
An experimental layout manager and formspec API replacement for Luanti (formerly Minetest). Vaguely inspired by Flutter and GTK.

Luanti's built-in way of describing menus (inventories, chests, dialogs, ...) is called a formspec. A formspec is a long string made of elements such as buttons, text fields, and inventory slots, and you have to give every element its exact position and size by hand. Flow lets you describe a menu with Lua tables instead, positions and sizes everything for you, and generates the formspec itself, so you never have to write one.

Online tutorial/demo (source)

docs.title: Layouting
docs.text:
• No manual positioning of elements.
  • Automatic layouting using HBox and VBox containers
  • Some elements have an automatic size.
  • The size of elements can optionally expand to fit larger spaces
  • Elements which get their size based on their label length automatically become larger/smaller to fit long translations1.

docs.title: Other features
docs.text:
• No form names. Form names are still used internally, however they are hidden from the API.
  • No having to worry about state.
  • Values of fields, scrollbars, checkboxes, etc are remembered when redrawing a form and are automatically applied.
  • Has an inspector mod to help with developing and debugging forms.
  • Some common security issues with formspec input handling are mitigated.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• This mod doesn't support all of the features that regular formspecs do. See Features flow does not have for a list.
  • FS51 is required if you want to have full support for Luanti 5.3 and below.
  • Make sure you're using the latest version of flow if you are on MT 5.10-dev or later, older versions used a hack which no longer works.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Flow ignores potentially malicious formspec input from clients, such as buttons or fields that haven't been shown to the client, out-of-bounds dropdown selections, and newlines in Field elements (where it's impossible to enter a newline without pasting it in).

docs.title: Other formspec libraries/utilities
docs.text:
These utilities likely aren't compatible with flow.

  • fs_layout is another mod library that does automatic formspec element positioning.
  • fslib is a small mod library that lets you build formspec strings.
  • Just_Visiting's formspec editor is a Luanti (sub)game that lets you edit formspecs and preview them as you go
  • kuto is a formspec library that has some extra widgets/components and has a callback API. Some automatic sizing can be done for buttons.
  • It may be possible to use kuto's components with flow somehow as they both use formspec_ast internally.
  • kuto was the the source of the "on_event" function idea.
  • My web-based formspec editor lets you add elements and drag+drop them, however it doesn't support all formspec features.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The official documentation is available at https://luk3yx.gitlab.io/minetest-flow/. Some code snippets have a "run" button which will open them in a web-based playground, not all of these will work properly as the playground doesn't support all formspec elements.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
This page describes the elements (widgets) that draw something or accept input. Elements that only arrange other elements (gui.VBox, gui.HBox, gui.Stack, ...) are described in Layouting elements.

Every element is a function in flow.widgets that takes a table of parameters:

local gui = flow.widgets

gui.Label{label = "Hello world!"}

The parameter lists below are generated automatically. Parameters marked -- Optional can be left out.

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text:
Sizes are measured in inventory slots: 1 is the width and height of one item slot. There is no hidden padding or spacing, so two boxes that are 1 wide and placed next to each other with spacing = 0 touch. You never give an element a position, boxes place their children and flow works out the total size of the form.

Elements that show text, such as labels, buttons, and fields, are sized to fit their text unless you give them a w and h. Elements that show something without a natural size, such as images, boxes, models, and tables, need an explicit w and h (their parameter lists below do not say -- Optional). Flow can only estimate the width of text because the real width depends on the player's font, screen size, and scaling settings, so avoid layouts that rely on exact text widths.

docs.title: Names and values
docs.text:
Many elements take a name. Input elements (fields, checkboxes, dropdowns, lists of text, tables, ...) with a name have their current value stored in ctx.form[name] and flow remembers it when the form is redrawn:

Element Value in ctx.form[name] gui.Field, gui.Pwdfield, gui.Textarea Text (string) gui.Checkbox true or false gui.Dropdown Text of the selected item, or its number if index_event = true gui.Textlist, gui.Table Number of the selected row (first row is 1)

Until the player changes something, the value is the element's initial value (default, selected, selected_idx), or "", false, or 1 if you did not give one. Text fields only send their text to the server when the player presses a button or Enter, so ctx.form can be out of date until then.

If your build function reads ctx.form.some_name, flow redraws the form automatically whenever the player changes that value (unless the element has its own on_event). Buttons do not store a value.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Elements that the player can use accept an on_event function, which is called with the player and ctx. Return true from it to redraw the form. A name is optional if you use on_event, flow makes one up.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text:
Colors are strings. "#RGB" and "#RRGGBB" are fully opaque, while "#RGBA" and "#RRGGBBAA" end with an alpha value, where 00 is fully transparent and FF is fully opaque. Color names also work (all the names from CSS, such as "red" and "darkgreen"), and you can add an alpha value after a #, for example "darkgreen#08".

Most text can also be coloured by putting color escape sequences in it, such as the ones made by core.colorize(). Dropdown items and tab captions are an exception, they cannot be coloured.

docs.title: Textures and items
docs.text: A texture name is the file name of an image from the textures folder of any loaded mod, such as "default_dirt.png". An item name is the registered name of an item or node, such as "default:dirt".

docs.title: Parameters shared by all elements
docs.text:
Every element, including layouting elements, accepts these parameters in addition to its own:

Parameter Description padding Space around the element, see Padding. visible Set to false to hide the element but keep its space, see Hiding elements. expand Set to true to make the element grow to fill spare space in the gui.HBox or gui.VBox it is in. If several elements expand, they share the spare space equally. align_h, align_v Where the element goes when there is more room than it needs: "start", "end", "center", "fill" (stretch), or "auto" (the default, flow picks one). "left" and "top" mean "start", "right" and "bottom" mean "end", and "center" means "center". min_w, min_h The smallest size of the element, for elements that size themselves. tooltip Text to show when the player hovers over the element, see Tooltips. style Inline styles, see Styling. on_event A function to call when the player uses the element, see Events above.

docs.title: Nine-slice images
docs.text:
Images and image-like backgrounds can optionally be drawn as a "nine-slice". The picture is cut into a 3x3 grid, where the corners keep their size, the edges are stretched in one direction, and the middle is stretched in both. This lets one small texture make a panel or border of any size without distorting its corners. The middle_* parameters describe where the cuts are, in texture pixels (whole numbers):

  • middle_x only: the cuts are middle_x pixels from every side.
  • middle_x and middle_y: middle_x pixels from the left and right sides and middle_y pixels from the top and bottom.
  • All four: the middle rectangle starts at middle_x, middle_y and ends at middle_x2, middle_y2. Negative middle_x2 and middle_y2 values are measured from the far (right/bottom) edge of the texture.

docs.title: gui.AnimatedImage
docs.text:
Shows an image that plays an animation. The texture must contain every frame stacked on top of each other (the first frame at the top), with all frames the same size. w and h are the size of one displayed frame.

middle_* parameters turn on nine-slice drawing, see Nine-slice images.

Example

gui.AnimatedImage{
    w = 1,
    h = 2,

    -- Only useful for styling.
    name = "my_animated_image", -- Optional

    -- Texture that contains all frames.
    texture_name = "texture.png",

    -- Number of frames in the texture.
    frame_count = 3,

    -- Milliseconds each frame is shown for. 0 means no animation.
    frame_duration = 4,

    -- Frame to start on, the first frame is 1. Default 1.
    frame_start = 5, -- Optional
    middle_x = 6, -- Optional
    middle_y = 7, -- Optional
    middle_x2 = 8, -- Optional
    middle_y2 = 9, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Background
docs.text:
Draws a picture behind everything else in the form: all backgrounds are drawn before any other element, whatever order they are in. The picture (texture_name) is stretched to w by h. If auto_clip is true, it is cut off at the edge of the form instead and w and h are ignored.

You usually do not need this element, set bgimg on a container or the root element instead (see Padding). Inside a gui.Stack, a gui.ScrollableVBox, or an embedded form, flow draws backgrounds without auto_clip as ordinary images.

Example

gui.Background{
    w = 1,
    h = 2,

    -- Picture to draw.
    texture_name = "texture.png",

    -- Cut off at the form edge, ignore w and h.
    auto_clip = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Background9
docs.text:
Like gui.Background, but the picture is drawn as a nine-slice so that it can be stretched to any size without distorting its corners.

Example

gui.Background9{
    w = 1,
    h = 2,

    -- Picture to draw.
    texture_name = "texture.png",

    -- Cut off at the form edge, ignore w and h.
    auto_clip = false,

    -- Nine-slice cut, see "Nine-slice images".
    middle_x = 3,
    middle_y = 4, -- Optional
    middle_x2 = 5, -- Optional
    middle_y2 = 6, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Bgcolor
docs.text:
Sets the colors behind the form. This does the same thing as the bgcolor, fbgcolor, and bg_fullscreen options of the root element, which are explained in Experimental features and are easier to use. fullscreen can be false, true, "both", or "neither".

Example

gui.Bgcolor{
    -- Background color of the form.
    bgcolor = "#FF0000",

    -- false, true, "both", or "neither".
    fullscreen = false, -- Optional

    -- Color of the area behind the form.
    fbgcolor = "#FF0000", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Box
docs.text:
Draws a solid rectangle of one color. Boxes have no natural size, so give them a w and h.

Unlike everywhere else, a hexadecimal color without an alpha value, such as "#FF0000", is drawn semi-transparent here. Add the alpha value ("#FF0000FF") to make it opaque.

Example

gui.Box{
    w = 1,
    h = 2,

    -- Fill color.
    color = "#FF0000",
}

docs.title: gui.Button
docs.text:
A clickable button showing label. Your on_event function is called when it is clicked. If you do not set w and h, the button is sized to fit the label (but never smaller than 1.6 by 0.8).

Buttons do not store a value in ctx.form.

Example

gui.Button{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ButtonExit
docs.text:
A button that closes the form when it is clicked. Your on_event function is still called before the form closes. In all other respects it works like gui.Button.

Example

gui.ButtonExit{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button_exit", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ButtonURL
docs.text:
A button that, when clicked, offers the player the choice of opening url in their web browser. url must start with http:// or https://. Your on_event function is also called. In all other respects it works like gui.Button.

Example

gui.ButtonURL{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button_url", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Web address to offer to open.
    url = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: gui.ButtonUrlExit
docs.text:
Like gui.ButtonURL, but the form also closes when the button is clicked.

Example

gui.ButtonUrlExit{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_button_url_exit", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Web address to offer to open.
    url = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: gui.Checkbox
docs.text:
A tick box with a text label. selected sets whether it starts ticked. If you give it a name, ctx.form[name] is true or false and is updated as soon as the player ticks or unticks it.

Checkboxes are sized automatically and do not accept w or h.

Example

gui.Checkbox{
    name = "my_checkbox", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
    selected = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Container
docs.text:
A group of elements that you position yourself with x and y instead of letting flow lay them out. See Manual positioning.

Example

gui.Container{
    w = 6, h = 2, -- Optional
    {type = "box", x = 0, y = 0, w = 1, h = 1, color = "red"},
    {type = "label", x = 1, y = 1.5, label = "Hello world!"},
}

docs.title: gui.Dropdown
docs.text:
A drop-down list that shows the currently selected item and lets the player pick another one from items (a list of strings). selected_idx is the number of the item that is selected at first (the first item is 1).

ctx.form[name] is the text of the selected item. If index_event = true it is the number of the selected item instead, which is easier to work with when two items have the same text or when the text is translated.

If you do not set w and h, the dropdown is sized to fit its longest item (but never smaller than 2 by 0.8). Item text cannot be coloured.

Example

gui.Dropdown{
    w = 2, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_dropdown", -- Optional

    -- List of choices.
    items = {"Hello world!", ...},

    -- Number of the item selected at first.
    selected_idx = 3, -- Optional

    -- Store the item number in ctx.form instead of its text.
    index_event = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Field
docs.text:
A single-line text box. label, if set, is shown above the box (flow leaves room for it automatically). default is the text it starts with.

ctx.form[name] is the text in the box. Newlines and other control characters are removed from it (a player can only get them into a field by pasting). The text is sent to the server when the player presses a button or Enter. To react to Enter, see Handling enter keypresses in fields.

If you do not set w and h, the field is sized to fit its default text and label (but never smaller than 3 by 0.8).

Example

gui.Field{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_field", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Text the field starts with.
    default = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Called when the player presses Enter.
    on_key_enter = function(player, ctx) end, -- Optional

    -- Close the form on Enter. Default false.
    close_on_enter = false, -- Optional

    -- Make "Done" on the mobile on-screen keyboard act like Enter.
    enter_after_edit = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.FieldCloseOnEnter
docs.text:
Sets whether pressing Enter in the field with this name closes the form. You normally do not need this element, as gui.Field has a close_on_enter parameter (and by default Enter does not close the form).

Example

gui.FieldCloseOnEnter{
    -- Name of the field.
    name = "my_field_close_on_enter",
    close_on_enter = false,
}

docs.title: gui.FieldEnterAfterEdit
docs.text:
Experimental, and only affects Android. If enter_after_edit is true, pressing "Done" in the text input dialog of the field with this name counts as pressing Enter. You normally do not need this element, as gui.Field has an enter_after_edit parameter.

Example

gui.FieldEnterAfterEdit{
    -- Name of the field.
    name = "my_field_enter_after_edit",
    enter_after_edit = false,
}

docs.title: gui.Hypertext
docs.text:
Shows text that can be formatted (bold, colors, different sizes, images, ...) and can contain clickable links. The text is written in a small HTML-like language, which is described in Hypertext markup. w and h are the size of the area that the text is wrapped to fit in.

If the markup contains <action name=...> links, ctx.form[name] is set to "action:" followed by the action name when the player clicks one. This behaviour is experimental and may change.

Example

gui.Hypertext{
    w = 6,
    h = 2,

    -- Receives the clicked action, see above.
    name = "my_hypertext", -- Optional

    -- Formatted text, see "Hypertext markup".
    text = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: gui.Image
docs.text:
Shows a picture, stretched to fit w by h. If you want to use one small texture for pictures of many sizes, use the middle_* parameters, see Nine-slice images.

Example

gui.Image{
    w = 4,
    h = 2,

    -- Texture to draw.
    texture_name = "texture.png",
    middle_x = 3, -- Optional
    middle_y = 4, -- Optional
    middle_x2 = 5, -- Optional
    middle_y2 = 6, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ImageButton
docs.text:
A button that is drawn as a picture instead of the usual button face. The picture (texture_name) is stretched to w by h, and label is drawn on top of it. It works like gui.Button otherwise.

  • noclip: Allow the button to be drawn outside the form's area.
  • drawborder: Draw the normal button border around the picture.
  • pressed_texture_name: Picture to show while the button is held down.

Example

gui.ImageButton{
    w = 6,
    h = 2,

    -- Picture to draw as the button.
    texture_name = "texture.png",
    name = "my_image_button", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
    noclip = false, -- Optional
    drawborder = false, -- Optional
    pressed_texture_name = "texture.png", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ImageButtonExit
docs.text:
Like gui.ImageButton, but the form also closes when the button is clicked.

Example

gui.ImageButtonExit{
    w = 6,
    h = 2,

    -- Picture to draw as the button.
    texture_name = "texture.png",
    name = "my_image_button_exit", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
    noclip = false, -- Optional
    drawborder = false, -- Optional
    pressed_texture_name = "texture.png", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ItemImage
docs.text:
Shows the picture that is used for an item or node in inventories (item_name, such as "default:dirt"), stretched to fit w by h.

Example

gui.ItemImage{
    w = 2,
    h = 3,

    -- Registered item or node name.
    item_name = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: gui.ItemImageButton
docs.text:
A button that shows the inventory picture of an item or node (item_name). By default, the item's description is shown as a tooltip when the player hovers over the button, which you can replace with the tooltip parameter. It works like gui.Button otherwise.

Give every item image button its own unique name, otherwise its tooltip may not work.

Example

gui.ItemImageButton{
    w = 1,
    h = 2,

    -- Registered item or node name.
    item_name = "Hello world!",
    name = "my_item_image_button", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Label
docs.text:
Shows text. Labels do not wrap long lines automatically: use \n to start a new line and do not use labels for long paragraphs. For those, use gui.Hypertext, or a gui.Textarea without a name (which wraps its text and gets a scrollbar if the text is too long).

Labels are sized to fit their text, and flow ignores color escape sequences when it estimates the width. To make the text bigger or smaller, use the font_size style (for example style = {font_size = "*2"}), see Styling.

Example

gui.Label{
    label = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: gui.List
docs.text:
Shows a grid of inventory slots, with the items of one inventory list in it. This is how you show the player's inventory, a chest, a furnace's input slots, and so on.

  • inventory_location: Which inventory to show. Common values are "current_player" (the inventory of the player who has the form open), "nodemeta:X,Y,Z" (the inventory of the node at that position, for example "nodemeta:10,5,-3"), and "detached:name" (a detached inventory). "player:name" is the inventory of a specific player and is only ever sent to that player.
  • list_name: The name of the list inside that inventory, such as "main" or "craft".
  • w and h: How many slots wide and high to draw (whole numbers).

Slots are filled from left to right, then top to bottom, and the player can move items in and out of them. The list is only shown if the inventory has been sent to the player's client. Only as many slots as the inventory list has are drawn, even if w times h is larger.

Each slot is 1 by 1, with 0.25 between slots, so a list that is 8 slots wide and 4 high is 9.75 by 4.75 big. To change the slot size or spacing, use the size and spacing styles, see Styling.

Example

gui.List{
    -- Which inventory to show.
    inventory_location = "Hello world!",

    -- Which list in that inventory to show.
    list_name = "Hello world!",
    w = 1,
    h = 2,

    -- Index of the first slot to draw. Unlike most numbers here, this starts
    -- at 0. Default 0.
    starting_item_index = 3, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Listcolors
docs.text:
Sets the colors of inventory slots. It is invisible, takes up no space, and should come before the gui.List elements it is for.

  • slot_bg_normal: Background color of a slot.
  • slot_bg_hover: Background color of a slot while the mouse is over it.
  • slot_border: Color of the border of the slots.
  • tooltip_bgcolor: Default background color of item tooltips.
  • tooltip_fontcolor: Default text color of item tooltips.

Only the first two are required. To use pictures instead of colors for slots, see Features flow does not have.

Example

gui.Listcolors{
    -- Slot background color.
    slot_bg_normal = "#FF0000",

    -- Slot background color when hovered.
    slot_bg_hover = "#FF0000",

    -- Slot border color.
    slot_border = "#FF0000", -- Optional

    -- Default tooltip background color.
    tooltip_bgcolor = "#FF0000", -- Optional

    -- Default tooltip text color.
    tooltip_fontcolor = "#FF0000", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Listring
docs.text:
Sets where items go when the player shift-clicks them. Every gui.Listring{inventory_location = ..., list_name = ...} adds a list to a ring, and shift-clicking an item in one list of the ring moves it to the next list in the ring. The first time a list appears in the ring decides which inventory the items are sent to.

gui.Listring{} with no parameters adds the last two gui.List elements that came before it. It is invisible and takes up no space.

Example

gui.Listring{
    -- Same as for gui.List.
    inventory_location = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Same as for gui.List.
    list_name = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Model
docs.text:
Shows a 3D model that the player can turn around with their mouse.

  • mesh: File name of the model, from the models folder of any loaded mod.
  • textures: The textures for the model, one for each of the model's materials in order.
  • rotation_x and rotation_y: How far the model is turned at first, in degrees.
  • continuous: Keep the model rotating by itself.
  • mouse_control: Whether the player can rotate the model with their mouse. Defaults to true.
  • frame_loop_begin and frame_loop_end: The range of animation frames to play. Defaults to all frames.
  • animation_speed: Frames per second to play the animation at. Defaults to 0 (no animation).

name is optional and only useful for styling.

Example

gui.Model{
    w = 5,
    h = 3,

    -- Only useful for styling.
    name = "my_model", -- Optional

    -- Model file name.
    mesh = "Hello world!",

    -- One texture for each material of the model.
    textures = {"texture.png", ...},

    -- Starting rotation in degrees.
    rotation_x = 3, -- Optional

    -- Starting rotation in degrees.
    rotation_y = 4, -- Optional

    -- Keep rotating by itself. Default false.
    continuous = false, -- Optional

    -- Let the player rotate the model. Default true.
    mouse_control = false, -- Optional

    -- First animation frame to play.
    frame_loop_begin = 5, -- Optional

    -- Last animation frame to play.
    frame_loop_end = 6, -- Optional

    -- Frames per second. Default 0.
    animation_speed = 7, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Pwdfield
docs.text:
A single-line text box for passwords: what the player types is hidden. It works like gui.Field, apart from not having a default. ctx.form[name] is the text that was typed. on_key_enter is supported, see Handling enter keypresses in fields.

Example

gui.Pwdfield{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_pwdfield", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Called when the player presses Enter.
    on_key_enter = function(player, ctx) end, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ScrollContainer
docs.text:
An area of a fixed size that clips the elements inside it and moves them when a scrollbar is moved. You usually want gui.ScrollableVBox instead, which does all of this for you. The elements inside are positioned by hand with x and y, like in gui.Container.

  • w and h: The size of the visible area.
  • scrollbar_name: The name of the gui.Scrollbar that controls the area. You need to add that scrollbar yourself.
  • orientation: "vertical" (the default) or "horizontal".
  • scroll_factor: How far the contents move for each step of the scrollbar's value. Default 0.1. It cannot be negative.

Flow cannot work out the range of the scrollbar for you here. Set max and thumbsize with gui.ScrollbarOptions before the scrollbar, where max is the height that is hidden divided by scroll_factor.

Example

gui.HBox{
    gui.ScrollContainer{
        w = 4, h = 3,
        scrollbar_name = "my_scrollbar",
        orientation = "vertical",
        {type = "label", x = 0, y = 0.5, label = "Top"},
        {type = "label", x = 0, y = 7.5, label = "Bottom"},
    },

    -- The contents are 8 high and 3 are visible, so 5 are hidden. This
    -- is 50 scroll steps of 0.1 each.
    gui.ScrollbarOptions{opts = {max = "50", thumbsize = "19"}},
    gui.Scrollbar{
        w = 0.5, h = 3,
        orientation = "vertical",
        name = "my_scrollbar",
    },
}

docs.title: gui.Scrollbar
docs.text:
A slider that the player can drag. ctx.form[name] is its position, a whole number from min to max (by default 0 to 1000, change them with gui.ScrollbarOptions before the scrollbar). value is the position it starts at, and orientation is "vertical" or "horizontal". Use it with a gui.ScrollContainer, or by itself as a slider.

scrollbar_bg, slider, arrow_up, and arrow_down are textures that replace the parts of the scrollbar. They are not described in the Luanti documentation and may be ignored.

Example

gui.Scrollbar{
    w = 8,
    h = 2,

    -- "vertical" or "horizontal".
    orientation = "vertical",
    name = "my_scrollbar", -- Optional

    -- Starting position.
    value = 3, -- Optional

    -- Texture. Optional, see above.
    scrollbar_bg = "texture.png", -- Optional

    -- Texture. Optional, see above.
    slider = "texture.png", -- Optional

    -- Texture. Optional, see above.
    arrow_up = "texture.png", -- Optional

    -- Texture. Optional, see above.
    arrow_down = "texture.png", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.ScrollbarOptions
docs.text:
Sets the options of the gui.Scrollbar elements that come after it. It is invisible and takes up no space. opts is a table with any of these options, all values are strings that contain whole numbers (except arrows):

  • min: The smallest value (default 0).
  • max: The largest value (default 1000). If it is the same as min, the scrollbar is disabled.
  • smallstep: How much the value changes when an arrow is clicked or the mouse wheel is scrolled (default 10). A negative number resets it to 10.
  • largestep: How much the value changes for Page Up and Page Down (default 100). A negative number resets it to 100.
  • thumbsize: The size of the thumb (the part that is dragged), counted in values out of the range of the scrollbar. For a scrollbar from 1 to 100, a thumbsize of 10 makes the thumb a tenth of the scrollbar long. If it is zero or less, it is reset to 1.
  • arrows: "show" or "hide" the arrow buttons. "default" hides them if the scrollbar gets too small, and shows them otherwise.

Example

gui.ScrollbarOptions{
    opts = {min = "0", max = "100", smallstep = "5", arrows = "hide"},
}

docs.title: gui.SetFocus
docs.text:
Gives keyboard focus to the element with this name. Put it before that element. Normally the focus is not changed when the form is shown again (for example by form:update()), so that the focus the player chose is kept. Set force to true to move the focus every time.

Checkboxes, buttons (of all kinds), tables, text lists, dropdowns, fields, password fields, text areas, and scrollbars can be focused.

Example

gui.SetFocus{
    -- Name of the element to focus.
    name = "my_set_focus",

    -- Move the focus every time. Default false.
    force = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Style
docs.text:
Sets style properties of elements by their name. See Styling. It is invisible and takes up no space.

Example

gui.Style{
    selectors = {"my_button"},
    props = {bgcolor = "red", textcolor = "yellow"},
}

docs.title: gui.StyleType
docs.text:
Sets style properties of every element of a type. See Styling. It is invisible and takes up no space.

Example

gui.StyleType{
    selectors = {"button", "image_button"},
    props = {textcolor = "yellow"},
}

docs.title: gui.Tabheader
docs.text:
A row of tabs. captions is the text of each tab, ctx.form[name] is the number of the selected tab (the first tab is 1), and current_tab is the tab that is selected at first. Showing the right contents for the selected tab is up to you, usually by reading ctx.form[name] in your build function.

Give it both a w and an h: flow cannot work out how much space it needs. If transparent is true the tabs are semi-transparent, and draw_border draws a thin line along the bottom of the tabs.

Example

gui.Tabheader{
    h = 1,
    name = "my_tabheader", -- Optional

    -- Text of each tab.
    captions = {"Hello world!", ...},

    -- Tab selected at first, the first is 1.
    current_tab = 2, -- Optional

    -- Draw semi-transparent. Default false.
    transparent = false, -- Optional

    -- Draw a line along the tabs. Default false.
    draw_border = false, -- Optional
    w = 3,
}

docs.title: gui.Table
docs.text:
A table with rows and columns that scrolls if it has too many rows. The player can select one row, and ctx.form[name] is the number of the selected row (the first row is 1). selected_idx is the row that is selected at first.

cells is one flat list with the text of every cell, going left to right along each row and then down to the next row. The number of columns comes from gui.TableColumns (the default is one text column). Put gui.TableColumns and gui.TableOptions before the table, as they only affect the table that comes after them. They do not take up any space.

Tables have no natural size, so you must give them a w and h.

Example

gui.Table{
    w = 3,
    h = 2,
    name = "my_table", -- Optional

    -- Text of every cell, row by row.
    cells = {"Hello world!", ...},

    -- Row selected at first, the first row is 1.
    selected_idx = 3, -- Optional
}

Example with columns and options

gui.VBox{
    gui.TableColumns{
        tablecolumns = {
            {type = "text", opts = {width = "8"}},
            {type = "text", opts = {align = "right"}},
        },
    },
    gui.TableOptions{
        opts = {highlight = "#335577"},
    },
    gui.Table{
        w = 10, h = 4,
        name = "scores",
        cells = {
            "Alice", "10",
            "Bob", "7",
        },
    },
}

docs.title: gui.TableColumns
docs.text:
Sets the columns of the gui.Table that follows it. tablecolumns is a list with one {type = ..., opts = {...}} entry for each column, from left to right. type is one of:

  • "text": Show the cell contents as text.
  • "image": The cell contents are a number that picks an image, which you set with the options ["0"] = "texture.png", ["1"] = "other.png", and so on (the numbers do not have to be consecutive). Empty cells and cells that are not numbers use image 0. Images are scaled down to fit the height of the row if necessary.
  • "color": The cell contents are a color that is used for the text of the next column(s). Use the span option to set how many columns it affects (default: all remaining columns).
  • "indent": The cell contents are a number that sets how far the next column is indented.
  • "tree": Like "indent", but the player can open and close the indented rows, like in a file browser.

opts is a table of options, all values are strings:

  • align: For text and image columns, where the content goes in the cell: "left" (default), "center", "right", or "inline".
  • width: For text and image columns, the minimum width, in "em" units (relative to the font size, default 0). For indent and tree columns, how far each level is indented (default 1.5).
  • padding: Space to the left of the column, in "em" units (default 0.5, or 0 for indent columns).
  • tooltip: Text to show when hovering over the column.

Example

gui.TableColumns{
    tablecolumns = {
        {type = "text", opts = {width = "8"}},
        {type = "text", opts = {align = "right"}},
    },
}

docs.title: gui.TableOptions
docs.text:
Sets the appearance of the gui.Table that follows it. opts is a table with any of these options, all values are strings:

  • color: Default text color (default "#FFFFFF").
  • background: Background color of the table (default "#000000").
  • border: "true" or "false", whether to draw a border (default "true").
  • highlight: Background color of the selected row (default "#466432").
  • highlight_text: Text color of the selected row (default "#FFFFFF").
  • opendepth: How many levels of "tree" column rows are open at first. Rows deeper than this are collapsed (default "0").

Example

gui.TableOptions{
    opts = {
        background = "#222222",
        highlight = "#335577",
        border = "false",
    },
}

docs.title: gui.Textarea
docs.text:
A multi-line text box. Long lines are wrapped to fit the width, and a scrollbar is added if the text is too tall. label, if set, is shown above the box and default is the text it starts with. ctx.form[name] is the text in the box, including its newlines.

If you leave out name, the text cannot be edited and no box is drawn, which makes it a label that wraps text and scrolls. Because it wraps, you should set a w and h for this.

Example

gui.Textarea{
    w = 6, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_textarea", -- Optional
    label = "Hello world!", -- Optional

    -- Text the box starts with.
    default = "Hello world!", -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Textlist
docs.text:
A list of text rows that scrolls if there are too many to fit. The player can select a row, and ctx.form[name] is the number of the selected row (the first row is 1). selected_idx is the row that is selected at first.

listelems is the text of each row. To color a row, start it with #RRGGBB (six hexadecimal digits). To start a row with a literal #, write ##. If transparent is true, no background is drawn behind the list.

Example

gui.Textlist{
    w = 1, -- Optional
    h = 2, -- Optional
    name = "my_textlist", -- Optional

    -- Text of each row.
    listelems = {"Hello world!", ...},

    -- Row selected at first, the first row is 1.
    selected_idx = 3, -- Optional

    -- Do not draw a background. Default false.
    transparent = false, -- Optional
}

docs.title: gui.Tooltip
docs.text:
Sets the text that is shown when the player hovers over another element, and optionally the colors of that tooltip. gui_element_name is the name of that element. Put the tooltip after the element it belongs to. It is invisible and does not take up any space.

If you only need to add some text, use the tooltip parameter on the element itself, see Tooltips.

Example

gui.Tooltip{
    -- Text to show.
    tooltip_text = "Hello world!",

    -- Background color of the tooltip.
    bgcolor = "#FF0000", -- Optional

    -- Text color of the tooltip.
    fontcolor = "#FF0000", -- Optional

    -- Name of the element to attach to.
    gui_element_name = "my_button",
}

docs.title: gui.Vertlabel
docs.text:
Shows text vertically, with one letter below the other, from top to bottom.

Example

gui.Vertlabel{
    label = "Hello world!",
}

docs.title: Experimental features
docs.text: These features might be broken in the future.

docs.title: no_prepend
docs.text:
Games and mods can add extra content to the start of every form shown to a player with player:set_formspec_prepend(), for example to give all forms the same background or style. This is called a "prepend", and it can be why a form has a background or style you did not expect.

You can set no_prepend = true on the "root" element to stop prepends from being applied to a form.

Example:

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox{
        no_prepend = true,

        gui.Button{label = "Button 1"},

        -- There will be an empty space where the second button would be
        gui.Button{label = "Button 2", visible = false},

        gui.Button{label = "Button 3"},
    }
end)

docs.title: bgcolor
docs.text:
You can set bgcolor = "#123", fbgcolor = "#123", and bg_fullscreen = true on the root element to set background colors:

  • bgcolor: The color of the background of the form itself.
  • fbgcolor: The color of the fullscreen background, which covers the whole screen behind the form.
  • bg_fullscreen: Which of the two colors to draw. false (the default) only draws bgcolor, true only draws fbgcolor, "both" draws both, and "neither" draws neither.

Colors that you leave out are not changed. See Elements for how colors are written.

docs.title: Putting the form somewhere else on the screen (likely required for most HUDs)
docs.text:
These values allow the position of the displayed form to be moved around and adjust how it is scaled.

Example:

local my_gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox{
        -- window_position is the point on the screen where the form is
        -- placed, and window_anchor is the point on the form that is put
        -- there. For both, 0 is the top/left and 1 is the bottom/right, and
        -- the default is {x = 0.5, y = 0.5} (the center).
        -- You probably want to set `window_position` and `window_anchor` to
        -- the same value.
        -- This puts the form in the bottom-right corner.
        window_position = {x = 1, y = 1},
        window_anchor = {x = 1, y = 1},

        -- Minimum space to leave around the form, as a fraction of the
        -- screen size (here 10% on the left/right and 20% at the top/bottom).
        -- If the form is too big, it will be scaled down. 0 lets the form
        -- touch the edge of the screen and negative values let it go off
        -- the edge.
        -- Default for forms: {x = 0.05, y = 0.05} (i.e. 5% of screen size)
        -- HUDs default to a hardcoded pixel size, if you want them to roughly
        -- line up with formspecs then you may explicitly specify this.
        window_padding = {x = 0.1, y = 0.2},

        gui.Label{label = "Hello world"},
    }
end)

docs.title: Rendering to a formspec
docs.text:
This API should only be used when necessary and may have breaking changes in the future.

Luanti describes menus with formspec strings, which flow normally generates and shows for you. Some APIs in other mods, such as sfinv, expect formspec strings instead. You can use this API to embed flow forms inside them. To use flow with these mods, you can call form:render_to_formspec_string(player, ctx, standalone).

  • A complete formspec starts with a formspec_version[] element (the version of the formspec language it uses) and a size[] element (the size of the form). By default these aren't included in the returned formspec, and are returned in a third value instead: a table info with w and h (the size of the form, in the units described in Elements) and formspec_version (the version number). Set standalone to include them in the returned formspec string. The third return value will not be returned.
  • Returns formspec, process_event[, info]
  • The process_event(fields) callback will return true if the formspec should be redrawn, where render_to_formspec_string should be called and the new process_event should be used in the future. This function may return true even if fields.quit is sent.

Warning: Do not use this API with node meta formspecs (formspecs that are stored in the metadata of a node), it can and will break!

docs.title: Embedding a form into another form
docs.text:
You can embed form objects inside others like this:

local parent_form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox{
        gui.Label{label = "Hello world"},
        other_form:embed{
            -- You can optionally pass in the player object to support older
            -- versions of flow (before 2025-06-17).
            player = player,

            -- A name for the embed. If this is specified, the embedded form
            -- will get its own context (accessible at ctx.my_embed_name) and
            -- field names will be rewritten to avoid conflicts with the
            -- parent form. If name is not specified, the embedded form will
            -- share ctx and ctx.form with the parent, and will not have field
            -- names rewritten.
            name = "my_embed_name",
        },
    }
end)

Special characters (excluding - and _) are not allowed in embed names.

docs.title: Running code when a form is closed
docs.text:
gui.Container, gui.HBox, gui.VBox, and gui.Stack elements support an on_quit callback which gets run when a player closes a form (for example by pressing Escape or clicking an exit button).

Note that this function is not called in some cases, such as when the player leaves without closing the form or when another form/formspec is shown.

This function must not return anything, behaviour may get added to return values in the future.

local parent_form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox{
        on_quit = function(player, ctx)
            core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(), "Form closed!")
        end,
    }
end)

If multiple on_quit callbacks are specified in different elements, they will all get called.

docs.title: Handling enter keypresses in fields
docs.text:
gui.Field and gui.Pwdfield support an on_key_enter callback that gets called if enter is pressed:

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox{
        gui.Field{
            label = "Press enter!",
            name = "field",
            on_key_enter = function(player, ctx)
                core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(),
                    "Field value: " .. dump(ctx.form.field))
            end,

            -- Pressing enter does not close the form by default. You can
            -- specify close_on_enter to close it when enter is pressed.
            -- This only applies to gui.Field.
            close_on_enter = true,
        },
    }
end)

Notes:

  • If you're using this callback, please make sure there's some other way to trigger the enter action (like a button) to support older flow versions and in case I replace this API with a better one in the future.
  • If you want recent mobile clients to call this callback when editing text, add enter_after_edit = true to the field definition. Without it, pressing "Done" on the on-screen keyboard of an Android device does not count as pressing enter. This is experimental.
  • The similarly named on_event gets called whenever the client submits the field to the server, which could be at any time, and is not very useful, but is still supported for compatibility (and there may be uses for it, such as sanitising field values). Be careful not to accidentally use the wrong callback.

docs.title: Getting a reference to the current player and context
docs.text:
If you're making a custom widget, it might be useful to get a reference to ctx and player so you don't have to pass them in manually.

local function HelloWorld(def)
    local ctx, player = flow.get_context()
    return gui.Label{
        label = "Hello, " .. player:get_player_name() .. "!\n" ..
            "some_value=" .. ctx.some_value,
        style = def.style,
    }
end

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    ctx.some_value = 123
    return HelloWorld{style = {font_size = "*2"}}
end)

flow.get_context() will error when called outside a build function (as you should not normally do this).

docs.title: gui.Flow container
docs.text:
gui.Flow is a fixed-width container that wraps items around if they don't fit. Unlike other elements, you must specify a width, and some options like min_w and padding aren't supported.

This is similar to GTK's FlowBox, but with a lot fewer features.

gui.Flow{
    -- Fits 3 items
    w = 3 * (1 + 0.2),

    gui.Image{w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "default_mese_crystal.png"},
    gui.Image{w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "default_mese_crystal.png"},
    gui.Image{w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "default_mese_crystal.png"},
    gui.Image{w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "default_mese_crystal.png"},
    gui.Image{w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "default_mese_crystal.png"},
}

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: A form is a menu that is shown to a player. It is made of elements (also called widgets), such as labels, buttons, text fields, and inventory slots, which are arranged by layout elements like gui.VBox. You describe a form with a build function that returns the elements, and flow works out the positions and sizes and shows the form for you. See Elements for what each element does.

docs.title: Basic example
docs.text:
See example.lua for a more comprehensive example which demonstrates how layouting and alignment works.

local gui = flow.widgets -- local recommended for direct referencing
local STARTING_SELECTION = 3 -- change and rerun to see the difference

local function build_vbox(player_obj, ctx)
    return gui.VBox {
        gui.Label {label = "Here is a dropdown:"},
        gui.Dropdown {
            name = "cool_dropdown",
            items = {'First item', 'Second item', 'Third item'},
            index_event = true,
            selected_idx = ctx.value or 1
        },
        gui.Button {
            label = "Get dropdown index",
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                local idx = ctx.form.cool_dropdown or ctx.value or 1
                core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(),
                    ("You have selected item #%d!"):format(idx))
            end,
        }
    }
end

local form = flow.make_gui(build_vbox)
local player_obj = core.get_player_by_name("playground")

form:show(player_obj, {value = STARTING_SELECTION}) -- second argument is optional

docs.title: Updating forms
docs.text:
If some data displayed inside a form changes (for example a timer or progress indicator), you can use form:update to update the form without resetting ctx or showing the form again if the player has closed it.

Luanti has no way to change a form that is already open, so flow has to show the whole form again. Because of this, players may lose text typed into fields that hasn't been sent to the server (which happens when they press a button or Enter) when form:update is called.

-- Re-shows the form for one player if they have the form open
my_gui:update(player)

-- Re-shows the form for all players that have the form open and where
-- ctx.test == 123
my_gui:update_where(function(player, ctx)
    return ctx.test == 123
end)

-- Re-shows the form for all players with the "server" privilege
my_gui:update_where(function(player, ctx)
    return core.check_player_privs(player, "server")
end)

-- Re-shows the form for all players with the form open
my_gui:update_where(function() return true end)

Inside an on_event handler, you can use return true instead.

gui.Button{
    label = "Update form",
    on_event = function(player, ctx)
        return true
    end,
}

If you're using a form as a HUD, you must call form:show_hud to update it.

docs.title: Hiding elements
docs.text: Elements inside boxes can have visible = false set to hide them from the player. Elements hidden this way will still take up space like with visibility: hidden; in CSS.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.VBox{
    gui.Button{label = "First button"},
    gui.Button{label = "Hidden", visible = false},
    gui.Button{label = "Last button"},
}

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: If you don't want hidden elements to take up any space, see the documentation for gui.Nil.

docs.title: Hypertext markup
docs.text:
gui.Hypertext shows text that is written in a small markup language with tags that look like HTML tags. It can be used to make text bold, coloured, bigger, or centred, to add pictures, and to add clickable links.

Warning: The markup language is currently unstable and may change. Use it with caution. Flow passes the text to Luanti without looking at it, so everything on this page is handled by the player's Luanti client, not by flow.

gui.Hypertext{
    w = 8, h = 3,
    text = "<center><big>Welcome!</big></center>" ..
        "This is <b>bold</b>, <i>italic</i>, and " ..
        "<style color='red'>red</style> text.",
}

What flow does not have: the markup can only be used in gui.Hypertext. Luanti can also show it in a tooltip (hypertip[]), but flow has no element for that, see Features flow does not have. Colors in the markup are written like colors everywhere else, see Colors.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Some tags enclose text: they open with <tagname> and close with </tagname>. Tags can have attributes, which are written in the opening tag as key=value. Attribute values should be quoted with either " or '. Inside a Lua string that is already in double quotes, use single quotes, as in <style color='red'>.

To write a literal <, >, or \ in the text, put a backslash before it. In a quoted attribute value, put a backslash before a literal quote mark. In Lua code, each backslash has to be written twice ("\\<"), or you can use a long string ([[\<]]).

docs.title: <style color=... font=... size=...>...</style>
docs.text:
Changes the style of the text inside it.

  • color: Text color.
  • size: Text size.
  • font: Text font, mono or normal.

docs.title: <global ...>
docs.text:
Sets the style of the whole text. You only need to use it once. If you put several in the text, their changes are made in the order the tags appear.

Attributes that only apply to the whole text:

  • background: Background of the text, a color or none.
  • margin: Space around the edge of the text, in pixels.
  • valign: Vertical alignment of the text: top, middle, or bottom.

Attributes that are inherited by everything inside the text:

  • color: Default text color.
  • hovercolor: Color of <action> links while the mouse is over them.
  • size: Default text size.
  • font: Default font, mono or normal.
  • halign: Default horizontal alignment: left, right, center, or justify.

docs.title: <tag name=... color=... hovercolor=... font=... size=...>
docs.text:
Defines a new tag, or changes the style of an existing one.

  • name: The name of the tag to define or change.
  • color: Text color.
  • hovercolor: Text color while the mouse is over it (only for action tags).
  • size: Text size.
  • font: Text font, mono or normal.

docs.title: Layout tags
docs.text:
These tags are always available. You can add more with <tag ...>.

Tag Effect <normal>...</normal> Normal size text <big>...</big> Big text <bigger>...</bigger> Bigger text <center>...</center> Centred text <left>...</left> Left-aligned text <right>...</right> Right-aligned text <justify>...</justify> Justified text <mono>...</mono> Monospaced font <b>...</b>, <i>...</i>, <u>...</u> Bold, italic, and underlined text

docs.title: <action name=...>...</action>
docs.text:
Makes the text inside it clickable. name is required. An optional url attribute is a web address to open when the text is clicked.

When the player clicks it, the form is sent to the server and the value of the gui.Hypertext element is "action:" followed by the action name. In flow, give the element a name and an on_event function, and read the value from ctx.form. This is experimental and may change.

gui.Hypertext{
    w = 6, h = 1,
    name = "help",
    text = "Read the <action name='rules'>rules</action>.",
    on_event = function(player, ctx)
        if ctx.form.help == "action:rules" then
            core.chat_send_player(player:get_player_name(), "No rules!")
        end
    end,
}

docs.title: <img name=... float=... width=... height=...>
docs.text:
Draws a texture that is in the client's media cache.

  • name: The name of the texture (required).
  • float: If present, the picture floats to the left or right and the text flows around it.
  • width, height: Force a size instead of using the size of the texture. If you only give one of them, the shape of the texture is kept.

docs.title: <item name=... float=... width=... height=... rotate=... angle=...>
docs.text:
Draws the inventory picture of an item.

  • name: The item name (required), such as default:dirt.
  • float, width, height: Like for <img>.
  • rotate: Make the item turn. Either yes or X,Y,Z, the rotation speeds around each axis as percentages of the standard speed (-1000 to 1000).
  • angle: The angle the item is shown at, as X,Y,Z, the angles around each of the three axes.

rotate and angle only work if the player has the inventory_items_animations setting turned on.

docs.title: Using a form as an inventory
docs.text:
Consider using Sway instead if you want to use flow as an inventory replacement while still having some way for other mods to extend the inventory.

A form can be set as the player inventory, which is the screen the player sees when they open their inventory. Flow internally generates the formspec (the text Luanti uses to describe a menu) and passes it to player:set_inventory_formspec(). This will completely replace your inventory and isn't compatible with inventory mods like sfinv (the inventory in Minetest Game, which lets mods add tabs).

local example_inventory = flow.make_gui(function (player, context)
    return gui.Label{ label = "Inventory goes here!" }
end)
core.register_on_joinplayer(function(player)
    example_inventory:set_as_inventory_for(player)
end)

Like with the show_hud function, update* functions don't do anything, so to update it, call set_as_inventory_for again with the new context. If the context is not provided, it will reuse the existing context.

example_inventory:set_as_inventory_for(player, new_context)

While the form will of course be cleared when the player leaves, if you'd like to unset the inventory manually, call :unset_as_inventory_for(player), analogue to close_hud:

example_inventory:unset_as_inventory_for(player)

This will set the inventory formspec string to "" and stop flow from processing inventory formspec input.

docs.title: Layouting elements
docs.text:
You should do local gui = flow.widgets in your code to improve readability. All examples will assume that this line exists.

These elements control how other elements are arranged. Most of them draw nothing themselves: they place the elements inside them, work out how big everything is, and share out any spare space. Elements that draw something or accept input (labels, buttons, fields, ...) are described in Elements. To place elements at exact coordinates instead, see Manual positioning.

Warning: The below elements (except gui.Spacer) do not support w and h properties and will break in weird ways if you try and use them. Use min_w and min_h instead.

docs.title: gui.VBox
docs.text:
A vertical box, similar to a VBox in GTK. Elements inside a VBox are stacked vertically.

gui.VBox{
    -- These elements are documented later on.
    gui.Label{label="I am a label!"},

    -- The second label will be positioned underneath the first one.
    gui.Label{label="I am a second label!"},
}

Elements inside boxes have a spacing of 0.2 between them. To change this, you can add spacing = <number> to the box definition. For example, spacing = 0 will remove all spacing between the elements.

docs.title: gui.HBox
docs.text:
Like gui.VBox but stacks elements horizontally instead.

gui.HBox{
    -- These elements are documented later on.
    gui.Label{label="I am a label!"},

    -- The second label will be positioned to the right of first one.
    gui.Label{label="I am a second label!"},

    -- You can nest HBox and VBox elements
    gui.VBox{
        gui.Image{w=1, h=1, texture_name="default_dirt.png", align_h="center"},
        gui.Label{label="Dirt", expand=true, align_h="center"},
    }
}

docs.title: gui.ScrollableVBox
docs.text:
Similar to gui.VBox, but shows its contents in an area of a fixed size that the player can scroll, and automatically adds a scrollbar next to it. Anything outside the area is hidden until it is scrolled into view. The area is w by h, both are optional: the width defaults to the width of the contents and the height defaults to the height of the contents, up to a maximum of 5.

On clients too old to support scrolling areas (before Luanti 5.4), flow shows one page of the contents at a time instead, with < and > buttons to change page.

To change how the scrollbar looks, set custom_scrollbar to a table of parameters for gui.Scrollbar, for example custom_scrollbar = {w = 0.8} to make it wider.

gui.ScrollableVBox{
    -- A name must be provided for ScrollableVBox elements. You don't
    -- have to use this name anywhere else, it just makes sure flow
    -- doesn't mix up scrollbar states if one gets removed or if the
    -- order changes.
    name = "vbox1",

    -- Specifying a height is optional but is probably a good idea.
    -- If you don't specify a height, it will default to
    -- min(height_of_content, 5).
    h = 10,

    -- These elements are documented later on.
    gui.Label{label="I am a label!"},

    -- The second label will be positioned underneath the first one.
    gui.Label{label="I am a second label!"},
}

docs.title: gui.Spacer
docs.text:
A "flexible space" element that expands by default. Example usage:

gui.HBox{
    -- These buttons will be on the left-hand side of the screen
    gui.Button{label = "Cancel"},
    gui.Button{label = "< Back"},

    gui.Spacer{},

    -- These buttons will be on the right-hand side of the screen
    gui.Button{label = "Next >"},
    gui.Button{label = "Confirm"},
}

I advise against using spacers when expand = true and align = ... would work just as well since spacers are implemented hackily and won't account for some special cases.

You can replicate the above example without spacers, however the code doesn't look as clean:

gui.HBox{
    -- These buttons will be on the left-hand side of the screen
    gui.Button{label = "Cancel"},
    gui.Button{label = "< Back", expand = true, align_h = "left"},

    -- These buttons will be on the right-hand side of the screen
    gui.Button{label = "Next >"},
    gui.Button{label = "Confirm"},
}

You should not use spacers to center elements as it creates unnecessary boxes, and labels may be slightly off-center (because label widths depend on screen size, DPI, etc and this code doesn't trigger the centering hack):

-- This is bad!
gui.HBox{
    gui.Spacer{},
    gui.Label{label="I am not properly centered!"},
    gui.Spacer{},
}

You should do this instead:

gui.Label{label="I am centered!", align_h = "center"},

This applies to other elements as well, because using HBox and Spacer to center elements creates unnecessary containers.

docs.title: gui.Nil
docs.text:
A tool to allow for ternary-ish conditional widgets:

local form = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    local the_boolean = false
    return gui.VBox{
        gui.Label{label = "The box below is only present if the boolean is truthy"},
        the_boolean and gui.Box{w = 1, h = 1, color = "#FF0000"} or gui.Nil{},
    }
end)

Use sparingly, flow still has to process each Nil object to be able to know to remove it, and thus could still slow things down. The fastest element is one that doesn't exist, and thus doesn't need processing.

docs.title: gui.Stack
docs.text:
This container element places its children on top of each other. All child elements are expanded in both directions.

Note that some elements (such as centred labels) won't pass clicks through to the element below them.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
gui.Stack{
    min_w = 10,
    gui.Button{label = "Hello world!"},
    gui.Image{w = 1, h = 1, texture_name = "air.png", padding = 0.2, align_h = "left"},
}

docs.title: gui.PaginatedVBox
docs.text:
Like gui.ScrollableVBox, but splits the contents into pages instead of scrolling. Only one page is shown at a time, with a < button, a "Page 1 of 3" label, and a > button underneath to change page. It needs a unique name, and w and h work the same way as for gui.ScrollableVBox. Elements are never cut in half: an element that does not fit on a page starts the next one.

gui.ScrollableVBox uses this automatically on clients that cannot scroll.

docs.title: gui.Padding (deprecated)
docs.text: Wraps a single element to add padding around it. It is deprecated and logs a warning, use the padding parameter of the element itself instead, see Padding.

docs.title: Dynamic element types
docs.text:
This is only recommended for elements inside gui.Container (see below) outside of some rare use cases that need it, as it does not support flow's layouting elements.

If you want to generate element types from a variable, you can use {type = "label", label = "Hello world!"} instead of gui.Label{label="Hello world!"}. The type is the name of the gui function in lowercase with underscores between words, for example "item_image_button" for gui.ItemImageButton. HBoxes and VBoxes can be created this way as well (with type = "hbox" and type = "vbox"), however other layouting elements (such as ScrollableVBox and Spacer) won't work correctly.

An example of this is in example.lua.

docs.title: Manual positioning of elements
docs.text:
You can use gui.Container elements to contain manually positioned elements. Every element inside a container has an x and y, which is the distance of its top-left corner from the top-left corner of the container, in the same units as w and h. Containers can be nested, in which case the offsets add up. If you do not give a w and h, flow uses the smallest size that fits all the elements inside.

gui.VBox{
    gui.Label{label = "Automatically positioned"},
    gui.Container{
        -- You can specify a width and height if you don't want flow to try and
        -- guess at the size of the container.
        -- w = 3, h = 2,

        -- You may embed most plain element tables (a `type`, an `x` and `y`,
        -- and the same parameters as the matching gui function) in a container
        {type = "box", x = 0, y = 0, w = 1, h = 1, color = "red"},
        {type = "box", x = 0.3, y = 0.3, w = 1, h = 1, color = "green"},
        {type = "box", x = 0.6, y = 0.6, w = 1, h = 1, color = "blue"},

        {type = "label", x = 2, y = 1.1, label = "Manually positioned"}
    },
}

Note that you should not nest layouted elements (like gui.VBox) inside gui.Container.

docs.title: Features flow does not have
docs.text: Flow does not support everything that Luanti formspecs can do. This page lists what is missing, so you know before you look for it. Where there is a way to get a similar result, it is mentioned.

docs.title: Missing elements
docs.text: Formspec element What it does What to do instead hypertip[] A tooltip that shows formatted text (see Hypertext markup). Flow tooltips only show plain text with the tooltip parameter or gui.Tooltip. The markup language can only be used in gui.Hypertext. allow_close[] Stops the Escape key (and similar) from closing the form. Nothing. Players can always close a flow form. You can run code when they do with on_quit, but you cannot stop it. listimages[] Pictures for the background of inventory slots. gui.Listcolors only sets colors. label[x,y;w,h;text] A label that wraps long text inside a given size (an "area label"). gui.Textarea without a name, or gui.Hypertext. Because of this, the halign and valign styles do not do anything for gui.Label. tooltip[x,y;w,h;...] A tooltip for an area instead of an element. The tooltip parameter of any element (flow uses the area of an element without a name for you). gui.Tooltip can only be attached to a named element. field[name;label;default] A small form with a single field and an automatic "Proceed" button (for example for signs). Use a gui.Field and a gui.Button.

docs.title: Missing parameters
docs.text:
• Content padding of scroll containers. Luanti can work out the range of a scroll container's scrollbar for you, but flow's gui.ScrollContainer does not expose this, so you have to set the range yourself with gui.ScrollbarOptions. gui.ScrollableVBox already does this for you.
  • Node formspec inventory locations. The "current_node" inventory location refers to the node whose formspec is open. A flow form cannot be the formspec of a node, so use "nodemeta:X,Y,Z" to show a node's inventory instead.

docs.title: Things flow does for you
docs.text:
These formspec elements exist, but flow generates them itself and you cannot write them:

  • size[]: The size of the form is worked out from the elements in it.
  • position[], anchor[], and padding[]: Use the window_position, window_anchor, and window_padding options of the root element, see Experimental features.
  • no_prepend[] and bgcolor[]: Use the no_prepend, bgcolor, fbgcolor, and bg_fullscreen options of the root element.
  • real_coordinates[]: Flow always uses the newer coordinate system, where there is no hidden padding or spacing between elements.
  • container_end[] and scroll_container_end[]: Elements inside gui.Container and gui.ScrollContainer are written inside the table.
  • formspec_version[]: Flow always uses formspec version 7.

docs.title: Newer Luanti features
docs.text: Because flow always uses formspec version 7 (Luanti 5.8), features that were added in newer versions may not work, even if the missing element or parameter is not listed above. This includes the area label (version 9), floating-point animation frames in gui.Model (version 10), and the halign and valign styles of fields and text areas (version 11), and the editable style of checkboxes, dropdowns, and fields (version 12, the only addition in that version). Formspec versions are described in the "Formspec Version History" section of the Luanti API documentation.

docs.title: Padding, spacing, and backgrounds
docs.text:
All elements can have a padding value, which will add the specified amount of padding around the element. The "root" element of the form (the one returned by build_func) has a default padding of 0.3, everything else has a default padding of 0.

HBox and VBox have a spacing field which specifies how much spacing there is between elements inside the box. If unspecified, spacing will default to 0.2.

Container elements (HBox and VBox) can optionally have bgimg and bgimg_middle parameters that specify a background for the container. bgimg is the name of a texture. If bgimg_middle is set, the texture is drawn as a nine-slice whose corners are bgimg_middle pixels big, so one small texture can make a background of any size. The background will be drawn behind any padding that the container has.

Example:

gui.VBox{
    padding = 0.5,
    spacing = 0.1,

    -- bgimg can be used without bgimg_middle
    bgimg = "air.png",
    bgimg_middle = 2,

    gui.Button{label="Button 1"},
    gui.Button{label="Button 2"},
}

The padding around the VBox is 0.5 and the spacing between the buttons inside it is 0.1.

docs.title: Popovers (highly experimental)
docs.text:
This API will likely have breaking changes in the future.

Flow supports a highly experimental low-level API for defining popovers. Popovers appear over top of all other elements and are anchored to their parent.

This API is intended to be used for creating themed widgets like dropdowns, or for a higher level popover API that adds styling and is easier to use.

You add a popover attribute to any container element to define a popover. Flow does not manage the lifecycle (opening/closing) of popovers, you must ensure that you do this yourself like in the example.

See the below example for details on how to use the API:

gui.VBox{
    -- Some padding is added for the purposes of the demo so that the popup
    -- isn't off-screen
    padding = 3,
    gui.Label{label = "Popover demo:"},

    gui.Stack{
        gui.Button{
            label = "Open popover",

            -- When the popover button is clicked, open the popover
            on_event = function(player, ctx)
                ctx.show_popover = true
                return true
            end,
        },

        -- The actual element to overlay
        -- "popover" is set to the gui.VBox element if (and only if)
        -- ctx.show_popover is true, otherwise it's nil so no popover is shown.
        popover = ctx.show_popover and gui.VBox{
            -- Specifying padding and bgcolor is optional, but is probably a
            -- good idea since flow doesn't do any styling on its own.
            padding = 0.2,
            bgcolor = "#222e",

            -- "side" specifies how the popover is positioned relative to the
            -- parent, and can be "bottom" (default), "top", "left", or "right".
            side = ctx.form.side,

            -- align_h and align_v align the popover according to its parent
            -- element. You only need to specify align_h for
            -- side = "top"/"bottom" or align_v for side = "left"/"right",
            -- this example specifies both so that it can demonstrate switching
            -- between different sides.
            align_h = "fill",
            align_v = "center",

            -- Popover contents
            gui.Label{label = "Hi there!"},
            gui.Dropdown{
                name = "side",
                items = {
                    "bottom",
                    "top",
                    "left",
                    "right",
                },
            },
        } or nil,

        -- Clicking outside the popover will call this function, which should
        -- probably close the popover.
        on_close_popover = function(player, ctx)
            ctx.show_popover = false
            return true
        end,
    },

    gui.Label{label = "After popover button"},
}

There are some restrictions on popovers:

  • They must not extend outside the form, otherwise they'll only be partially visible (unless everything is styled with noclip = true, see Styling). Flow does not attempt to detect this.
  • You can only define popover on container elements, like gui.Stack, gui.HBox, and gui.VBox.
  • Only one popover is shown at a time.
  • Players can still use tab to interact with things behind the popover, despite being unable to use their mouse to do so.
  • You cannot show popovers inside of other popovers.
  • Popovers cannot be on the root element.

docs.title: Styling forms
docs.text:
Styles change how elements look: their colors, images, fonts, and so on. A style is a set of properties such as bgcolor = "red", and which properties exist depends on the type of element. All of them are listed in the property reference below.

You can style a single element with the style field (the inline syntax), or style many elements at once with the gui.Style and gui.StyleType elements (see separate style elements).

docs.title: Inline syntax
docs.text:
At the moment I suggest only using this syntax if your form won't look broken without the style - older versions of flow don't support this syntax, and I may make breaking changes to the sub-style syntax in the future.

You can add inline styles to elements with the style field:

gui.Button{
    label = "Test",
    style = {
        bgcolor = "red",

        -- You can style specific states of elements:
        {sel = "$hovered", bgcolor = "green"},

        -- Or a combination of states:
        {sel = "$hovered, $pressed", bgcolor = "blue"},
        {sel = "$hovered+pressed", bgcolor = "white"},
    },
}

The properties directly inside style always apply. A sel entry only applies while the element is in one of the listed states. Separate states with a comma to apply the style when any of them is active ("$hovered, $pressed"), or join them with + to apply it only when all of them are active at once ("$hovered+pressed").

If you need to style multiple elements, you can reuse the style table:

local my_style = {bgcolor = "red", {sel = "$hovered", bgcolor = "green"}}

local gui = flow.make_gui(function(player, ctx)
    return gui.VBox{
        gui.Button{label = "Styled button", style = my_style},
        gui.Button{label = "Unstyled button"},
        gui.Button{label = "Second styled button", style = my_style},
    }
end)

Note that this may inadvertently reset styles on subsequent elements if used on elements without a name. Luanti can only style unnamed elements by their type, so flow applies the style to every element of that type and then resets those properties to their defaults straight after the element. This also undoes any earlier gui.StyleType for the same properties. Give the element a name to avoid this.

Property values are normally strings, but flow also accepts numbers and booleans where a property needs one. Setting a property to an empty string (bgimg = "") resets it to its default value.

docs.title: Separate style elements
docs.text:
Alternatively, you can use the gui.Style and gui.StyleType elements if you need to style a large group of elements or need to support older versions of flow:

gui.Style{
    selectors = {"btn1"},
    props = {
        bgimg = "button.png",
        border = false,
    }
},

gui.Button{
    name = "btn1",
    label = "Button",
},

The Style and StyleType elements are invisible and won't affect padding. They only affect the elements that come after them, so put them before the elements you want to style.

Warning: gui.Style and gui.StyleType do not support styles that change the element size, such as font_size for labels, buttons, and fields, and size/spacing for lists. Flow only sees these properties in the inline syntax, so use that for them.

docs.title: Selectors and states
docs.text:
selectors is a list that says which elements the style applies to:

  • gui.Style selects elements by their name, so {"btn1"} styles the element with name = "btn1".
  • gui.StyleType selects elements by their type, so {"button"} styles every button that comes after it. The type is the element's name in lowercase with underscores between words, for example item_image_button for gui.ItemImageButton. Some types also style other types, see element types.
  • gui.StyleType also accepts "*", which selects every element.

A selector can end with a colon and one or more states to only style the element while it is in that state, such as "btn1:hovered" or "button:hovered+pressed" (+ means all of the states have to be active).

gui.StyleType{
    selectors = {"button", "image_button"},
    props = {textcolor = "yellow"},
},
gui.StyleType{
    selectors = {"button:hovered"},
    props = {bgcolor = "#336699"},
},

docs.title: States
docs.text:
Every element has the default state, which is the same as not giving any state. Buttons (gui.Button, gui.ButtonExit, gui.ImageButton, gui.ItemImageButton) also have these states:

State Active when focused The button has keyboard focus hovered The mouse is over the button pressed The button is being pressed

docs.title: Element types
docs.text:
These are the types that can be styled. A type that "inherits" from another also uses the styles set for the other type, for example a style set on image also applies to animated_image.

Type Element Inherits from animated_image gui.AnimatedImage image box gui.Box button gui.Button button_exit gui.ButtonExit button checkbox gui.Checkbox dropdown gui.Dropdown field gui.Field image gui.Image image_button gui.ImageButton item_image_button gui.ItemImageButton label gui.Label list gui.List model gui.Model pwdfield gui.Pwdfield field scrollbar gui.Scrollbar tabheader gui.Tabheader table gui.Table textarea gui.Textarea textlist gui.Textlist vertlabel gui.Vertlabel label

Luanti also lists hypertip, but flow has no element for it, see Features flow does not have. gui.ItemImage has the item_image type, which only supports noclip (see Other elements). gui.ImageButtonExit and gui.ButtonURL are not in Luanti's list of types, so give them a name and style them with gui.Style or the inline syntax.

docs.title: Property reference
docs.text: Colors are described in Elements, and textures are image file names. A "2D vector" is written as a string such as "1,2". Properties that only list a type of element are not valid on other elements, and an unknown property is ignored.

docs.title: All elements
docs.text: Property Description noclip Boolean. Set to true to let the element be drawn outside the area of the form. Default false.

docs.title: Text properties
docs.text:
These properties change how text looks. font and font_size are valid on buttons, labels, fields, tables, and text lists. textcolor is valid on buttons, labels, fields, and tab headers, but not on tables and text lists. The sections below show which applies where.

Property Description font Font type, a comma-separated list. Use at most one of normal (the default font) and mono (a font where every letter is the same width), and any of bold and italic. For example "mono,bold". If you only give bold or italic, normal is used. Default normal. font_size Text size. "16" sets an absolute size, "+2" and "-2" make the text 2 points larger or smaller than the default, and "*1.5" multiplies the default size by 1.5 (like em in CSS). The default is the size the player has chosen in their settings. textcolor Color of the text. Default white.

Flow can make room for bigger text in gui.Labels, buttons, and the default text of fields, but only if font_size starts with * and is set with the inline syntax (style = {font_size = "*2"}). Other values still change the text but not the size of the element. The labels above fields and checkboxes ignore font_size, and a gui.Label with a fixed h is positioned as if font_size was not set (this is deprecated).

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text:
For gui.Button, gui.ButtonExit, gui.ImageButton, and gui.ItemImageButton. Buttons also support font, font_size, and textcolor.
